items.original_title: FinancialJuice: MUFG on ECB Rate Decision

evidence.headline: FinancialJuice: MUFG on ECB Rate Decision
evidence.snippet: Let’s start with the policy decision. The ECB held the deposit rate at 2.50%, as expected, with unchanged guidance. The statement highlighted both sides of the debate. There was emphasis on the larger and longer-lasting energy shock but also a new explicit reference to the impact from tighter financial conditions and the lack of second-round effects. That gave the statement a cautious tone but overall it reads like justification for a pause at this juncture rather than an argument against further tightening. That was certainly backed up by Lagarde’s comments in the Q&A. She revealed that, although the decision to hold was unanimous, policymakers debated whether to hike at this meeting and suggested that current conditions “could have warranted" further tightening. While stopping short of pre-committing to December, Lagarde’s remark that the ECB’s “direction of travel” is clear points to at least one more hike to come, barring significant developments or shocks. While market conditions were noted, there was little suggestion that higher market rates are viewed as a substitute for policy action. All told, given Lagarde’s comments, we see the decision as a hawkish pause which leaves the door wide open to further tightening. Our call remains that the ECB delivers a further 50bp of tightening, with 25bp hikes at the next projection meetings in December and March. That would push rates into mildly restrictive territory. In line with the ECB’s assessment, we still see relatively little evidence that energy prices are generating second-round effects. But the duration of the energy shock increases the risk that price pressures will broaden. That risk will become increasingly difficult to ignore and we continue to think the argument for further action will ultimately win

items.original_title: FinancialJuice: Goldman Sachs on AI Space

evidence.headline: FinancialJuice: Goldman Sachs on AI Space
evidence.snippet: Price action since mid-October has shown that there is a threshold beyond which Al-related cost-of-capital concerns can threaten the broader growth narrative. Over these past few weeks, this overhang has affected the non-AI landscape, with spreads decompressing (Le., lower rated cohorts underperforming) and correlations moving notably higher. And as our rates strategy colleagues have noted, the past few weeks have also catalyzed a rally in duration as Treasuries served as a hedge amid the risk-off tone. AI funding concerns, elevated yields, and escalating geopolitical tensions pushed USD credit spreads to break out (wider) from their local range. In the USD market, pairwise correlations of spread changes reached their highest level since the 1Q2026 Iran escalation (Exhibit 1). Meanwhile, sovereign stress in the Euro area has added to the risk-off tone, and EUR credit correlations have similarly risen.

items.original_title: FinancialJuice: MUFG on BoJ

evidence.headline: FinancialJuice: MUFG on BoJ
evidence.snippet: The yen has been volatile overnight with USD/JPY hitting a low of 157.12 after the BoJ’s policy decision, but it has since quickly given back those gains rising up to 157.70. At today's policy meeting the BoJ decided to leave the policy rate at 1.25% with only one dissenter. Hajime Takata voted in favour of a hike considering that that with underlying inflation having reached the price stability target, the situation had shifted to a new phase in which the Bank needs to step up the pace of policy tightening to bring the policy rate closer to the neutral rate. The main surprise in the policy statement was that the BoJ unanimously decided to sped p the pace of ETF sales. The annual pace of equity ETF sales will increase from JPY330 billion to JPY860 billion on a book-value basis from January 2027. As a share of total stock market trading value the sales will increase from 0.05% to 0.1% while the estimated period required to complete the sales of all ETF holdings will shorten from around 112 years to 43 years. It remains unclear why there was a need to suddenly increase the pace of selling.
